claim: SARS-CoV-2 has caused over 777 million COVID-19 cases and 7.1 million deaths as of March 2025.
source: The virus encodes 4 structural proteins, 16 nonstructural proteins (nsps) involved in replication and transcription, and several accessory proteins (ORFs) linked to immune evasion (V'kovski et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to the World Health Organization report mentioned in the text.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 encodes 4 structural proteins, 16 nonstructural proteins (nsps) involved in replication and transcription, and several accessory proteins (ORFs) linked to immune evasion.
source: The virus encodes 4 structural proteins, 16 nonstructural proteins (nsps) involved in replication and transcription, and several accessory proteins (ORFs) linked to immune evasion (V'kovski et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to V'kovski et al., 2021 and Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Many viruses, including Ebola, dengue, and reovirus, encode 2'-O-methyltransferases that mimic the host 5' cap structure to evade innate immune recognition.
source: Many viruses, including Ebola (Valle et al., 2021), dengue (Jung et al., 2018), and reovirus (Furuichi et al., 1975), encode 2'-O-methyltransferases (2'-O-MTases) that mimic the host 5' cap structure to evade innate immune recognition (Daffis et al., 2010; Züst et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to Valle et al., 2021; Jung et al., 2018; Furuichi et al., 1975; Daffis et al., 2010; and Züst et al., 2011.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 nsp16, in complex with nsp10, functions as a 2′-O-MTase, modifying capped viral RNA from 'cap-0' to 'cap-1'.
source: Similarly, SARS-CoV-2 nsp16, in complex with nsp10, functions as a 2′-O-MTase, modifying capped viral RNA from 'cap-0' to 'cap-1' (Benoni et al., 2021; Park et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Benoni et al., 2021 and Park et al., 2022.

claim: The cap-1 modification protects SARS-CoV-2 from host antiviral defenses, such as MDA5 recognition and IFIT1 restriction.
source: This modification protects the virus from host antiviral defenses, such as MDA5 recognition and IFIT1 restriction (Bergant et al., 2022; Russ et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bergant et al., 2022 and Russ et al., 2022.

claim: Nsp16 disrupts global host mRNA splicing, reducing cellular protein and mRNA levels.
source: Beyond immune evasion, nsp16 disrupts global host mRNA splicing, reducing cellular protein and mRNA levels (Banerjee et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Banerjee et al., 2020.

claim: Nsp16 enhances SARS-CoV-2 entry by upregulating TMPRSS2 expression.
source: Nsp16 also enhances SARS-CoV-2 entry by upregulating TMPRSS2 expression (Han et al., 2023), underscoring its role as a virulence factor.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Han et al., 2023.

claim: Nsp16-deficient SARS-CoV-2 strains exhibit low pathogenicity and elicit robust immune responses.
source: Notably, nsp16-deficient strains exhibit low pathogenicity and elicit robust immune responses, suggesting their potential as live-attenuated vaccines (Balieiro et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Balieiro et al., 2022.

claim: Inhibitors targeting nsp16 or the nsp16-nsp10 complex have been developed.
source: Given the critical functions of nsp16, inhibitors targeting nsp16 or the nsp16-nsp10 complex have been developed (Klima et al., 2022; Nguyen et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Klima et al., 2022 and Nguyen et al., 2023.

claim: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is a key pathway for targeted protein degradation.
source: The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) is a key pathway for targeted protein degradation, often described as 'the molecular kiss of death' (Tieroyaare Dongdem and Adiyaga Wezena, 2022; Park et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tieroyaare Dongdem and Adiyaga Wezena, 2022 and Park et al., 2020.

claim: Substrate ubiquitination involves a cascade of three enzymes: E1 activating enzyme, E2 conjugating enzyme, and E3 ubiquitin (Ub) ligase.
source: Substrate ubiquitination involves a cascade of three enzymes: E1 activating enzyme, E2 conjugating enzyme, and E3 ubiquitin (Ub) ligase (Zheng and Shabek, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zheng and Shabek, 2017.

claim: Over 600 E3 ligases are encoded in the human genome.
source: Over 600 E3 ligases encoded in the human genome regulate diverse cellular processes in response to various signals (; Garcia-Barcena et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Garcia-Barcena et al., 2020.

claim: E3 ligases are categorized into three classes: Really Interesting New Gene (RING), homologous to the E6AP carboxyl terminus (HECT), and RING-between-RING (RBR) ligases.
source: Based on conserved domains and Ub transfer mechanisms, E3 ligases are categorized into three classes: Really Interesting New Gene (RING), homologous to the E6AP carboxyl terminus (HECT), and RING-between-RING (RBR) ligases (Garcia-Barcena et al., 2020; Morreale and Walden, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Garcia-Barcena et al., 2020 and Morreale and Walden, 2016.

claim: RING E3 ligases transfer ubiquitin directly from the E2-Ub complex to substrates.
source: RING E3s transfer Ub directly from the E2-Ub complex to substrates (Deshaies and Joazeiro, 2009), whereas HECT-type E3s first attach Ub to their own catalytic cysteine before transferring it (Huibregtse et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Deshaies and Joazeiro, 2009.

claim: HECT-type E3 ligases first attach ubiquitin to their own catalytic cysteine before transferring it to substrates.
source: RING E3s transfer Ub directly from the E2-Ub complex to substrates (Deshaies and Joazeiro, 2009), whereas HECT-type E3s first attach Ub to their own catalytic cysteine before transferring it (Huibregtse et al., 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Huibregtse et al., 1995.

claim: MG132 treatment significantly increased the abundance of nsp8, nsp11, and nsp16 in HEK293T cells.
source: MG132 treatment significantly increased the nsp8, nsp11, and nsp16 abundance in HEK293T cells (Figure 1A), suggesting UPS-mediated degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nsp8 undergoes TRIM22-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation.
source: Nsp8 undergoes TRIM22-mediated ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation (Fan et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fan et al., 2024.

claim: Proteasome inhibitors Bortezomib and Carfilzomib enhanced nsp16 stability.
source: To confirm UPS-mediated nsp16 degradation, we tested additional proteasome inhibitors, Bortezomib and Carfilzomib, both of which enhanced nsp16 stability.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lysosomal inhibitors (Bafilomycin A1 and NH4Cl) and the autophagy-lysosomal inhibitor Vinblastine had no effect on nsp16 stability.
source: In contrast, lysosomal inhibitors (Bafilomycin A1 and NH4Cl) and the autophagy-lysosomal inhibitor, Vinblastine, had no such effect (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MG132 treatment significantly prolonged nsp16 stability, extending its half-life from 2 hr to 15 hr.
source: MG132 treatment significantly prolonged nsp16 stability, extending its half-life from 2 hr to 15 hr (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: KEGG pathway and Gene Ontology (GO) analyses revealed that inhibiting nsp16 degradation increased its interacting proteins, including 43 associated with viral processes, 22 involved in mRNA stability regulation, and 5 linked to cellular antiviral defense.
source: Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway and Gene Ontology (GO) analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) revealed that inhibiting nsp16 degradation increased its interacting proteins, including 43 associated with viral processes, 22 involved in mRNA stability regulation, and 5 linked to cellular antiviral defense.
evidence: The claim is supported by bioinformatics analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Six E3 ligases—UBR5, MARCHF7, HECTD1, TRIM32, MYCBP2, and TRIM21—were identified as nsp16-binding proteins.
source: Among them, 6 E3 ligases—UBR5, MARCHF7, HECTD1, TRIM32, MYCBP2, and TRIM21—were selected for further investigation.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data described in the text.

claim: UBR5 and MARCHF7 knockdown significantly stabilized nsp16 protein levels.
source: UBR5 and MARCHF7 knockdown significantly stabilized nsp16 protein levels (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Silencing UBR5 in MARCHF7 knockdown cells, and vice versa, further enhanced nsp16 stability, indicating that these ligases act independently.
source: Silencing UBR5 in MARCHF7 knockdown cells, and vice versa, further enhanced nsp16 stability, indicating that these ligases act independently (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Wild-type MARCHF7 and UBR5, but not their mutants lacking functional RING or HECT domains, effectively degraded nsp16 in knockdown cells.
source: Notably, wild-type MARCHF7 and UBR5, but not their mutants lacking functional RING (1–542 aa) or HECT domains, respectively, effectively degraded nsp16 in knockdown cells (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and 2E.

claim: Nsp16 undergoes ubiquitination both with and without exogenous ubiquitin expression.
source: We first confirmed nsp16 ubiquitination both with and without exogenous Ub expression (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claim: Silencing either UBR5 or MARCHF7 reduced nsp16 ubiquitination compared to the negative control.
source: Silencing either ligase reduced nsp16 ubiquitination compared to the negative control, indicating their involvement in this modification (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MARCHF7 primarily mediates K27-linked ubiquitination of nsp16.
source: Further analysis of lysine-specific linkages revealed that MARCHF7 primarily mediates K27-linked ubiquitination of nsp16, whereas UBR5 facilitates K48-linked ubiquitination (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: UBR5 facilitates K48-linked ubiquitination of nsp16.
source: Further analysis of lysine-specific linkages revealed that MARCHF7 primarily mediates K27-linked ubiquitination of nsp16, whereas UBR5 facilitates K48-linked ubiquitination (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: Co-IP experiments confirmed that Myc-tagged MARCHF7 and endogenous UBR5 bind to nsp16.
source: Co-IP experiments confirmed that Myc-tagged MARCHF7 and endogenous UBR5 bind to nsp16 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: FRET assays confirmed direct interactions between nsp16 and both UBR5 and MARCHF7.
source: When nsp16-YFP was bleached, the fluorescence intensity of CFP-UBR5 and CFP-MARCHF7 increased, confirming direct interactions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FRET experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: UBR5 and MARCHF7 independently bind to nsp16.
source: The interactions remained unchanged, indicating that UBR5 and MARCHF7 independently bind to nsp16 (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP experimental data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: UBR5 and MARCHF7 colocalized with nsp16 predominantly in the cytoplasm, with some nuclear colocalization observed in HeLa cells.
source: Immunofluorescence (IF) staining revealed that UBR5 and MARCHF7 colocalized with nsp16 predominantly in the cytoplasm, with some nuclear colocalization observed in HeLa cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: UBR5 and MARCHF7 both interacted with nsp16 and colocalized with PDI, but not with COX5A or GM130.
source: Notably, UBR5 and MARCHF7 both interacted with nsp16 and colocalized with PDI, but not with COX5A or GM130 (Figure 4C and D), indicating that both E3 ligases interact with nsp16 primarily in the ER.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: Only the HECT domain mutant of UBR5 failed to degrade nsp16.
source: Only the HECT domain mutant failed to degrade nsp16 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), consistent with previous studies (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B and a citation to Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: The HECT domain mutant of UBR5 lost the ability to ubiquitinate nsp16.
source: This mutant also lost the ability to ubiquitinate nsp16, confirming the essential role of the HECT domain in this process (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: All MARCHF7 truncation mutants lost the ability to degrade nsp16.
source: All mutants lost the ability to degrade nsp16 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Only the MARCHF7 mutant containing the intact N-terminal region (aa 1–542) strongly bound to nsp16.
source: Further analysis revealed that only the mutant containing the intact N-terminal region (aa 1–542) strongly bound to nsp16, while those retaining the active RING domain region (aa 543–616) did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Only wild-type MARCHF7 promoted K27-linked ubiquitination of nsp16.
source: Consistently, only wild-type MARCHF7 promoted K27-linked ubiquitination of nsp16 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Knockdown of either UBR5 or MARCHF7 significantly increased SARS-CoV-2 replication.
source: Knockdown of either UBR5 or MARCHF7 significantly increased SARS-CoV-2 replication, with simultaneous knockdown further enhancing viral replication (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Co-IP using an anti-nsp16 antibody confirmed its interaction with endogenous MARCHF7 and UBR5, along with ubiquitination, following infection with the IME-BJ01 strain.
source: Co-IP using an anti-nsp16 antibody confirmed its interaction with endogenous MARCHF7 and UBR5, along with ubiquitination (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by Co-IP experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Knockdown of either UBR5 or MARCHF7 in Caco2 cells significantly increased intracellular and secreted viral mRNA levels (M and E genes) for both IME-BJ01 and Omicron strains.
source: Knockdown of either E3 ligase in Caco2 cells significantly increased intracellular and secreted viral mRNA levels (M and E genes) for both strains.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C–E and 5F–H.

claim: Viral titers in the supernatants increased upon UBR5 or MARCHF7 knockdown, with UBR5 knockdown causing over a 1-log rise for the IME-BJ01 strain and even greater effects for Omicron.
source: Viral titers in the supernatants also increased, with UBR5 knockdown causing over a 1-log rise for the IME-BJ01 strain and even greater effects for Omicron (Figure 5C–E and F–H for the IME-BJ01 and Omicron strains, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C–E and 5F–H.

claim: Overexpression of UBR5 or MARCHF7 significantly reduced viral mRNA (M and E genes) and N protein levels in both IME-BJ01 and Omicron strains.
source: Overexpression significantly reduced viral mRNA (M and E genes) and N protein levels in both strains, accompanied by a 0.5-log decrease in viral titers.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A–H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–H.

claim: Co-transfection with increasing nsp16 levels counteracted the inhibitory effects of UBR5 or MARCHF7 overexpression on viral replication.
source: However, co-transfection with increasing nsp16 levels counteracted these inhibitory effects (Figure 6A–H, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A–H and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–H.

claim: Catalytically inactive mutants of UBR5 (UBR5-ΔHECT) or MARCHF7 (MARCHF7-aa 1–542) failed to suppress viral replication.
source: These mutants failed to suppress viral replication.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–H.

claim: Treatment with MG132 restored nsp16 protein levels for all tested variants.
source: Treatment with MG132 restored nsp16 protein levels for all variants (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B), confirming UPS-mediated degradation.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: UBR5 or MARCHF7 knockdown stabilized nsp16 proteins from various SARS-CoV-2 variants, though to varying degrees.
source: Furthermore, UBR5 or MARCHF7 knockdown stabilized nsp16 proteins from these variants, though to varying degrees (Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3C.

claim: MARCHF7 expression decreased consistently with increasing viral titers of IME-BJ01 and Omicron strains.
source: MARCHF7 expression decreased consistently with increasing viral titers, whereas UBR5 levels initially rose at low titers before declining as infection progressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A–C.

claim: UBR5 levels initially rose at low viral titers before declining as infection progressed.
source: MARCHF7 expression decreased consistently with increasing viral titers, whereas UBR5 levels initially rose at low titers before declining as infection progressed (Figure 6—figure supplement 4A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4A–C.

claim: UBR5 expression negatively correlated with disease progression in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients.
source: UBR5 expression negatively correlated with disease progression, whereas MARCHF7 levels showed no significant correlation (Figure 6—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from patient samples shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4D.

claim: MARCHF7 levels showed no significant correlation with disease severity in SARS-CoV-2-infected patients.
source: UBR5 expression negatively correlated with disease progression, whereas MARCHF7 levels showed no significant correlation (Figure 6—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from patient samples shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4D.

claim: E3 ligase overexpression significantly reduced viral E gene copy numbers in the lungs and markedly decreased viral titers in mice.
source: E3 ligase overexpression significantly reduced viral E gene copy numbers in the lungs and markedly decreased viral titers (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figures 7C and 7D.

claim: Mice treated with UBR5 or MARCHF7 experienced less weight loss compared to controls.
source: Additionally, treated mice experienced less weight loss compared to controls (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Lungs from UBR5- or MARCHF7-treated mice exhibited reduced alveolar contraction and pulmonary edema compared to control mice.
source: Histopathological analysis at 5 days post-infection showed that lungs from UBR5- or MARCHF7-treated mice exhibited reduced alveolar contraction and pulmonary edema compared to the severe lesions observed in control mice (Figure 7F).
evidence: The claim is supported by histopathological data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: UBR5 and MARCHF7 treatment significantly reduced the production of inflammatory cytokines including interleukin-6, interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, and interleukin-1β in the spleens of infected mice.
source: Consistent with their antiviral activity, UBR5 and MARCHF7 treatment significantly reduced the production of these inflammatory cytokines (Figure 7H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: High-resolution structures of nsp16 and nsp16-nsp10 heterodimers have been characterized.
source: High-resolution structures of nsp16 and nsp16-nsp10 heterodimers have been characterized (Rosas-Lemus et al., 2020; Klima et al., 2022; Lugari et al., 2010), providing a foundation for antiviral drug development targeting these complexes (Balieiro et al., 2022; Melo-Filho et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rosas-Lemus et al., 2020; Klima et al., 2022; and Lugari et al., 2010.

claim: Several host E3 ligases—such as RNF5, Cullin4-DDB1-PRPF19, ZNF598, and TRIM7—ubiquitinate and degrade key SARS-CoV-2 proteins, thereby suppressing viral replication.
source: Several host E3 ligases—such as RNF5, Cullin4-DDB1-PRPF19, ZNF598, and TRIM7—ubiquitinate and degrade key SARS-CoV-2 proteins, thereby suppressing viral replication (Li et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Maimaitiyiming et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2023; Liang et al., 2022; Maimaitiyiming et al., 2022; and Zhang et al., 2024.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 uses DUBs to counteract host defenses and enhance viral replication.
source: In contrast, SARS-CoV-2 uses DUBs to counteract these defenses and enhance viral replication (Chen et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2024; Gao et al., 2022; and Guo et al., 2021.

claim: Nsp16 is a short-lived protein with a half-life of only 2–3 hr.
source: In this study, we identify nsp16 as a short-lived protein with a half-life of only 2–3 hr, which is targeted for ubiquitination and degradation via the UPS.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: UBR5 is a member of the UBR box protein family and contains a HECT domain essential for its E3 ligase activity.
source: UBR5, a member of the UBR box protein family, contains a HECT domain essential for its E3 ligase activity (Kim et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2021.

claim: UBR5 targets the ORF4b protein of Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus for degradation, reducing its ability to counteract the host immune response.
source: For instance, UBR5 targets the ORF4b protein of Middle East respiratory syndrome coronavirus for degradation, reducing its ability to counteract the host immune response (Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2022.

claim: UBR5 supports Zika virus replication by assisting TER94/VCP in degrading the capsid protein, allowing viral genome release into the cytoplasm.
source: Conversely, UBR5 supports Zika virus replication by assisting TER94/VCP in degrading the capsid protein, allowing viral genome release into the cytoplasm (Gestuveo et al.).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gestuveo et al.

claim: MARCHF7 plays a role in T cell proliferation, neuronal development, inflammasome regulation, and tumor progression.
source: MARCHF7, a RING E3 ligase, plays a role in T cell proliferation, neuronal development, inflammasome regulation, and tumor progression (Zheng, 2021; Zhang et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zheng, 2021; Zhang et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2022; and Zhao et al., 2018.

claim: MARCHF7 has been identified as a host protein interacting with the 2C protein of foot-and-mouth disease virus.
source: However, its involvement in viral infections remains largely unexplored, with one study identifying it as a host protein interacting with the 2C protein of foot-and-mouth disease virus (Mahajan et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Mahajan et al., 2021.

claim: MS analysis identified K76 as a ubiquitination site on nsp16.
source: MS analysis identified K76 as a ubiquitination site (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The nsp16 K76R mutant still underwent degradation, though its ubiquitination level was reduced compared to that of the wild-type.
source: However, the nsp16 K76R mutant still underwent degradation, though its ubiquitination level was reduced compared to that of the wild-type, indicating that K76 is one of several ubiquitination sites (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D and E.

claim: High-pressure tail vein injection is a gene delivery method primarily targeting the liver but also effective for lung tissues.
source: To assess their antiviral effects in vivo, we used high-pressure tail vein injection, a gene delivery method primarily targeting the liver (Kamimura et al., 2014) but also effective for lung tissues (Bonamassa et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kamimura et al., 2014 and Bonamassa et al., 2011.

claim: Human trials using naked DNA injections have shown variable immune responses, with one case of fatal immune activation reported.
source: For instance, human trials using naked DNA injections (e.g. OTC cDNA) have shown variable immune responses, with one case of fatal immune activation reported (Raper et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Raper et al., 2003.

claim: UBR5 and MARCHF7 are two E3 ligases from distinct families—RING-type MARCHF7 and HECT-type UBR5—that independently target nsp16 for degradation.
source: Notably, two E3 ligases from distinct families—RING-type MARCHF7 and HECT-type UBR5—independently target nsp16 for degradation, disrupting its function and exhibiting strong antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: UBR5 induces K48-linked ubiquitination of nsp16.
source: UBR5 induces K48-linked ubiquitination, whereas MARCHF7 promotes K27-linked ubiquitination, independently suppressing SARS-CoV-2 replication in cell cultures and in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: MARCHF7 promotes K27-linked ubiquitination of nsp16.
source: UBR5 induces K48-linked ubiquitination, whereas MARCHF7 promotes K27-linked ubiquitination, independently suppressing SARS-CoV-2 replication in cell cultures and in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E and 3F.

claim: UBR5 and MARCHF7 independently suppress SARS-CoV-2 replication in cell cultures and in mice.
source: UBR5 induces K48-linked ubiquitination, whereas MARCHF7 promotes K27-linked ubiquitination, independently suppressing SARS-CoV-2 replication in cell cultures and in mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5, 6, and 7.

claim: UBR5 and MARCHF7 degrade nsp16 variants from different viral strains, exhibiting broad-spectrum antiviral activity.
source: Notably, UBR5 and MARCHF7 also degrade nsp16 variants from different viral strains, exhibiting broad-spectrum antiviral activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.
